blurb: Stout upright stems carrying big deep blue-to-purple tubes at a very usable border height — one of the most intensely coloured of the Colorado natives, and sturdy enough not to need staking.
water: Low; xeric — well-drained ground, no supplemental water once established
spread: Upright and clumping from a woody crown
seasons: Deep blue-purple tubular flowers in summer on stout stems; dies back to a basal crown in winter
wildlife: Tubular flowers worked by native bees and bumblebees; hummingbirds visit the genus

care.hardiness: A Colorado native that CSU lists as plantable to about 9,000 ft, so it is comfortably hardy at Boulder's zone 5b–6a — this is a plant of our own climate rather than an import being coaxed along.[2]
care.planting: Set out young container plants in spring after the mid-May last frost, into ground you have already made free-draining. Water thoroughly once at planting, then be sparing — CSU's warning is to water in well but avoid overwatering afterwards, which is how most new penstemons are killed. In a pot use a gritty mineral mix and a container deep enough for the taproot.[1]
care.sun: Full sun. CSU's rule for the genus is at least six hours of direct sun to get erect stems and clear, bright flower colour; in shade the stems stretch and the colour washes out.[1][2]
care.soil: Well-drained soil. It is a plant of dry slopes and open ground, so lean, gritty soil keeps the stems stout; rich, damp soil makes it soft and short-lived. Above all, CSU stresses that penstemons need excellent aeration and drainage and do poorly in compacted soil — a rock garden or xeriscape bed is the ideal, and heavy clay is the enemy.[1][2]
care.water: Low. The nuance worth knowing is CSU's: even penstemons considered completely drought tolerant still want good *spring* moisture, and it is watering *after* flowering that invites crown rot. So water it in spring and then leave it alone.[1]
care.spacing: Space about 15–18 in apart. The stems are notably stout and self-supporting, unlike the taller wand-type penstemons that can lean.[2]
care.propagation: By seed. Penstemon seed generally germinates best after a cold-moist period, so the simplest route is an autumn sowing outdoors that lets winter do the work. Deadheading to prolong the plant's life (below) does trade away the self-sown seedlings, so leave a few stalks if you want replacements.[1]
care.sow: Sow outdoors in fall onto a lean, gritty surface and leave the seed to chill naturally over winter; if starting indoors, give the seed several weeks of cold-moist stratification in the fridge first. Keep the seedbed on the dry side once germinated — seedlings rot as readily as adults.[1]
care.bloom: Flowers roughly June through mid-August in deep blue-purple tubular flowers in summer on stout stems.[2]
care.maintenance: Low. The one job that matters is deadheading: CSU notes that removing spent flower stalks before they set seed can increase a penstemon's lifespan, which is worth doing for a genus whose species are often short-lived. Cut old growth back in early spring rather than fall, and skip both fertilizer and compost mulch — lean is better.[1]
care.troubles: Crown and root rot in wet or compacted soil are the main killers, and they are cultural rather than bad luck. CSU also lists rust fungi, and grasshopper and flea beetle damage, as the common problems. Give it air movement, water at the base and not overhead, and don't crowd it.[1]

references.name: CSU Extension — Native Herbaceous Perennials for Colorado Landscapes (fact sheet 7.242, PDF: complete Table 1)

edible.summary: No documented culinary use; penstemons are grown as native ornamentals and pollinator plants.[1][2]
edible.caution: No authority consulted documents a food use for Penstemon glaber, so this guide treats it as inedible — don't eat it. No part is recorded as notably poisonous either, but an absent poisoning record is not evidence of edibility. Nothing in this genus is a food plant in this guide, so don't reason across from one penstemon to another.[1][2]
